name: The rounded stucco edge
symptom: A stucco or EIFS wall whose every edge — corners, reveals, the returns into openings, the top of a parapet — is a soft radius of 3/8 to 3/4 in produced by a plastic bullnose bead, on a building whose style wants a crisp cut edge. The wall looks like it was moulded rather than built, and no edge on it produces a hard line of shadow.

cause.explanation: Corner beads are a stock accessory sold in square, bullnose and 3/4 in radius profiles; bullnose is the default on the shelf because it resists chipping and it hides out-of-plumb framing, which a square bead ruthlessly exposes. In EIFS the substrate is foam, so a square arris is structurally fragile and the manufacturer's own guidance pushes toward a radius. The plasterer chooses the bead; nobody specifies it.
cause.cost_saved: Effectively nothing on the bead itself — square and bullnose beads cost within pennies of each other. What is saved is the framing tolerance: a square arris on stucco requires the corner to be straight and plumb to about 1/8 in in 8 ft, which is framing labour, roughly $0.60-$1.20 per lineal foot of corner.

rule_violated.ref: an arris is a light-behaviour decision, not a taste one
rule_violated.statement: A square arris divides a lit face from a shaded face across a single line; a radius creates a graded transition 3/8 to 3/4 in wide that reads as a highlight rather than an edge, and softens the whole elevation's contrast at every corner simultaneously.
These traditions require the opposite: rounded, soft arrises from hand-applied lime render over earth or rubble. Getting the arris backwards is the fault in EITHER direction.

correct_practice: Decide the arris from the tradition, then buy the bead to match. Hard-edged traditions — Italian Renaissance and its revivals, Beaux-Arts, Regency, Greek Revival stucco, Georgian stucco-on-brick, and anything with a scored ashlar or a run cornice — want a square arris of not more than about 1/16 in radius, with the render straight-edged and the corner true. Soft traditions — Pueblo Revival, New Mexico adobe, Spanish Colonial, Mexican hacienda, Cape Dutch, Andalusian and Mediterranean vernacular — want a hand-modelled arris of 1/2 to 2 in radius, formed by the plasterer's hand rather than by a bead, and irregular from corner to corner. The failure is applying either answer to the wrong tradition, and applying a MACHINE version of the soft answer — a uniform 3/4 in radius, identical at every corner — is a third failure: real hand-rounded render varies visibly along its own length.

fixes.right: Specify the bead: square-nose galvanised or PVC corner bead with the render brought straight to it for the hard traditions; no bead at all, wire lath carried round the corner and the render hand-floated, for the soft ones. Say it in the specification, because the plasterer will otherwise buy what the yard stocks.
fixes.cheap: Free, if caught before the lath goes on — it is a line in the spec and a different box off the same shelf. After the fact, the cheapest correction on a hard-edged building is to add real members at the edges where the arris matters most: a quoin strip, a plain pilaster, or a run band at the corners, which reintroduces a hard line without re-rendering the wall.
fixes.dishonest: Painting the corners a darker shade to sharpen them. A graded radius painted with a hard line puts the colour edge and the geometric edge in different places, which the eye resolves as a mistake rather than as an edge. Also dishonest, in the soft traditions: a uniform machined radius achieved by a bullnose bead, which produces the shape of hand work with none of its variation and reads at fifty feet as extruded.

detection: Zoom on any external corner in a photograph. A square arris shows a single-pixel-scale transition from lit to shaded value; a bullnose shows a bright band 3/8 to 3/4 in wide running the whole height of the corner, which at 40 ft reads as a white pinstripe on every corner of the house — that pinstripe is the most reliable signature of synthetic stucco in an image. Second test, for the soft traditions: measure the radius at three heights on the same corner. Genuinely hand-modelled render varies by a factor of two or more along a single corner; bead-formed render does not vary at all. Third: look at the window reveal returns. A bullnose at the reveal produces a rounded jamb with a visible bead line, and the sill will usually be caulked to it.

exceptions.why: Rounded corners and arrises are a defining characteristic and a crisp arris is the fault there.
exceptions.bounds: The radius must be substantial — 1 to 3 in — and hand-varied. A 3/8 in machine bullnose is not soft enough to read as adobe and is too soft to read as masonry; it lands in the gap and reads as neither.

bounds_test.note: A 3/8 in machine bullnose fails at the bottom of this range and is the specific failure mode worth naming: it is neither answer.

exceptions.why: Whitewash over a wall whose corners are visibly rounded and soft is the style's own diagnostic tell for plastered earth brick as against stone.
exceptions.bounds: Softness must extend to the whole surface — a slightly undulating wall plane, not a flat wall with rounded edges. A dead-flat EIFS wall with rounded corners is a different building.

bounds_test.note: Softness must extend to the whole surface — a slightly undulating wall plane, not a flat wall with rounded edges. A dead-flat EIFS wall with rounded corners is a different building.

exceptions.why: Annually limewashed lime render over 500-700 mm of tapia or rubble accumulates a soft arris by repeated coats; sharpness would be false.
exceptions.bounds: The softening is cumulative and greatest at the base and at reachable heights. Uniform softness at parapet level, where nobody's brush reaches, is a machine tell.

bounds_test.note: The softening is cumulative and reachable-height biased. A ratio near 1.0 means the radius was formed by a bead rather than accumulated by a brush.
Hand-floated lime render over mass wall.

exceptions.why: Deliberate irregularity, including rolled and undulating render, is the style's subject.
exceptions.bounds: Irregularity must be irregular. Uniform whimsy is a catalogue.

bounds_test.note: Irregularity must be irregular. Uniform whimsy is a catalogue.

confused_with.difference: Both are shadow failures, but this one removes the edge and that one removes the member. On a stucco wall you can have a correct 6 in surround and still lose it to a bullnose bead on every edge.

test.note: For the hard-edged traditions. A square arris divides lit from shaded across a single line; a bullnose bead grades the transition over 3/8-3/4 in and reads at 40 ft as a white pinstripe running the full height of every corner. That pinstripe is the most reliable signature of synthetic stucco in a photograph, and its measurable width IS the radius.

secondary_tests.note: Applies to the SOFT traditions and is the test that catches machine whimsy. Genuinely hand-modelled render varies by a factor of two or more along a single corner; bead-formed render does not vary at all. A uniform 3/4 in radius has the shape of hand work and none of its variation, and reads at fifty feet as extruded.
The photograph-available form of the primary test where the corner cannot be measured directly: the width of the specular band at the corner, against a known dimension elsewhere in the image.
